title: Chapter LV

teacherSummary.text: Bingley proposes to Jane, who is overjoyed. Mr. Bennet jokes that they are so easy-going every servant will cheat them. The family celebrates.

vocabulary.definition: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner
vocabulary.context: Kitty simpered and smiled, and hoped her turn was coming soon.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: An oration or eulogy in praise of some person or achievement
vocabulary.context: This naturally introduced a panegyric from Jane on his diffidence, and the little value he put on his own good qualities.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: The act of meditating or contriving beforehand
vocabulary.context: Jane instantly gave a look at Elizabeth, which spoke her distress at such premeditation, and her entreaty that she would not give into it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Your tempers are by no means unlike.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Her younger sisters soon began to make interest with her for objects of happiness which she might in future be able to dispense.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Deviating or departing from the center, or from the line of a circle
vocabulary.context: There was nothing of presumption or folly in Bingley that could provoke his ridicule, or disgust him into silence; and he was more communicative, and less eccentric than the other had ever seen him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Openly declared, avowed, acknowledged, or claimed
vocabulary.context: Bingley was everything that was charming, except the professed lover of her daughter.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Jane could have no reserves from Elizabeth, where confidence would give pleasure; and instantly embracing her, acknowledged, with the liveliest emotion, that she was the happiest creature in the world.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.context: Not a word, however, passed his lips in allusion to it, till their visitor took his leave for the night; but as soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter and said—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

vocabulary.definition: Possessed of genius, or the faculty of invention
vocabulary.context: But on returning to the drawing-room, when her letter was finished, she saw, to her infinite surprise, there was reason to fear that her mother had been too ingenious for her.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

significance: Jane's happiness rewards her patience and goodness.
discussionQuestions: Do Jane and Bingley deserve each other? Why?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LV,” how does Austen show happiness for Jane? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LV develops the idea of happiness for Jane. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter LV to complicate the reader's understanding of happiness for Jane. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of happiness for Jane responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of happiness for Jane. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Do Jane and Bingley deserve each other? Why? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include simpered, panegyric, premeditation, tempers, dispense. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Kitty simpered and smiled, and hoped her turn was coming soon.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To smile in a silly, affected, or conceited manner.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Engagements needed the father's consent. Now, why does this chapter matter? Jane's happiness rewards her patience and goodness. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot plot, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
segments.passage: She then sat still five minutes longer; but unable to waste such a precious occasion, she suddenly got up, and saying to Kitty, “Come here, my love, I want to speak to you,” took her out of the room. Jane instantly gave a look at Elizabeth, which spoke her distress at such premeditation, and her entreaty that she would not give into it.

segments.activity: Students complete the chapter quiz, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor.
segments.script: Now it is your turn. First, the chapter quiz in the app. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LV,” how does Austen show happiness for Jane? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference with you.

segments.activity: One-sentence claim plus one quoted piece of evidence.
segments.script: To close: in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about happiness for Jane, and back it with one short quotation. Hand it to me on your way out.
